did_you_know.text: Did you know? The opponents of the temple’s construction are called in the verse “the enemies of Judah and Benjamin,” and they heard that the exiles were building a temple for the LORD, the God of Israel.

Did you know? The opponents offered to join in the construction, claiming that they too worshiped the God of Israel and had sacrificed to him since the days of Esarhaddon, king of Assyria, who had settled them there.
Did you know? Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the heads of the families rejected the offer and made it clear that the Israelites would build alone, in accordance with the command of Cyrus, king of Persia.
Did you know? After being rejected, the people of the land tried to weaken the people of Judah and intimidate the builders in order to stop their work.
Did you know? The opposition continued throughout the reign of Cyrus, king of Persia, and into the reign of Darius, by hiring advisers to frustrate the builders’ plans.
Did you know? Beginning with verse 8, the chapter contains an official letter in Aramaic, sent by Rehum the commander, Shimshai the scribe, and their associates to Artaxerxes, king of Persia.
Did you know? Among the groups mentioned in the letter were peoples whom the great Osnappar deported and settled in the cities of Samaria and the rest of the region west of the Euphrates.
Did you know? The writers of the letter portrayed Jerusalem as a rebellious and wicked city, claiming that the Jews were rebuilding the city and repairing its walls.
Did you know? At the end of their claim, the writers warned that if Jerusalem were rebuilt and its walls completed, the king would lose his share of the region west of the Euphrates.
Did you know? As a result of the decree, the work on the temple of God in Jerusalem stopped, and it remained halted until the second year of the reign of Darius, king of Persia.
